title: Code-review radar for interviews (what seniors flag)
hook: Interview code review is a checklist in your head: async correctness, allocation hot paths, thread safety, API surface, nullability, and security at boundaries. This topic turns that radar into explicit signals interviewers listen for.

blocks.text: Code-review radar is the set of questions you ask on every pull request: Does this block the thread pool? Does it allocate in a loop? Is shared state synchronized? Are public types intentional? Are nullability warnings honest? Does SQS handler respect cancellation? Seniors trade off speed versus risk — they flag .Result, lock across await, and string concat in Redis paths immediately.

entries.plainDefinition: Blocking on Task.Result or .Wait() instead of awaiting.
entries.example: var data = GetDataAsync().Result; // starves thread pool

entries.plainDefinition: Message that always fails processing and must not infinite-retry.
entries.example: Malformed JSON — dead-letter after N attempts.

entries.plainDefinition: Code executed very frequently under production load.
entries.example: Redis cache read on every authenticated request.

blocks.text: System design interviews increasingly include 'review this code' slides. Naming the smell and the fix — single-flight cache, ConfigureAwait in library, IDisposable on native wrapper — demonstrates production experience. Radar connects modules 13–17 into one pass.

blocks.title: Review order
blocks.body: Correctness and security first, then concurrency, then allocations, then style.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: 1. Correctness and security
items.body: Auth on every endpoint. Input validation at boundary. No secrets in logs. Poison message handling with dead-letter.

items.title: 2. Async and cancellation
items.body: No .Result/.Wait. CancellationToken through SQS receive, HTTP, DB. OperationCanceledException handled on drain.

items.title: 3. Concurrency
items.body: No lock across await. ConcurrentDictionary or channels for shared state. Cache stampede — single-flight or lock per key.

items.title: 4. Memory and native
items.body: No ToList/string concat per message. Span/TryParse on hot paths. using on SkiaSharp/streams. ArrayPool return discipline.

items.title: 5. API and nullability
items.body: public types intentional. No null-forgiving without invariant. ApiCompat on libraries.

items.title: 6. Performance evidence
items.body: Claims need BenchmarkDotNet or dotnet-counters — not vibes. ValueTask only with measured sync-complete path.

snippet.explanation: First smell in async services — blocking wait on async method.

snippet.label: Flags: SQS handler without token
snippet.explanation: Queue consumers must observe host cancellation for graceful drain.

snippet.label: Flags: nullable lie
snippet.explanation: Suppressing nullability with ! without guard is a review reject.

blocks.title: Review smells
rows: sync fs, busy loops on main thread

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Nitpicking naming while missing .Result on hot path. Approving public types without API check. Ignoring allocation in code that runs per message on SQS.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: run the expanded checklist in order — security/correctness before naming. For SQS consumers, grep for .Result, missing CancellationToken, and ToList inside the receive loop. dotnet-counters on staging: thread-pool queue length + gen-0 rate validate allocation fixes. Interview 'review this code' slides: name the smell, cite the module fix, and state what you would measure before approving.

snippet.label: Expanded radar — cache stampede and allocation flags
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–8: three high-priority smells from the expanded checklist with module-linked fixes — async (13), span (17), concurrency (15).

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Nitpicking variable names while missing .Result on the hot path. Approving SQS handler without CancellationToken. Ignoring per-message ToList allocation. Reviewing style before correctness and security. Not connecting a smell to a concrete fix from the curriculum.

interviewTakeaways: Senior code review order: security/correctness → async/cancellation → concurrency → memory/native → API/nulls → measured perf.
Flag sync-over-async, lock across await, and per-message allocation before style nits.
Expanded checklist: poison messages, cache stampede, SkiaSharp using, ApiCompat on libraries.
60s: Correctness first. No Result. Token through SQS. Concurrent collections. Span not Split. using native. BenchmarkDotNet for perf claims.
Follow-up: how do you handle a poison SQS message without infinite retry?
commonPitfalls: Nitpicking naming while missing .Result on hot path gets you rejected in review interviews.
Missing cancellation in queue handlers — no graceful drain on deploy.
Strong answer: 'Six-step radar. Name smell, cite module fix, say what metric proves it — gen-0, thread-pool depth, or BenchmarkDotNet.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Same radar: async correctness, type honesty, resource cleanup — different syntax, same senior instincts.

sync fs.readFileSync in an Express handler is the JS analogue of .Result — blocks the loop like thread-pool starvation. C# review radar maps directly: non-blocking I/O, cancellation on shutdown, no alloc in per-request hot path.
